title: Ink on new paper (Avot 4:20)
hookLine: learning young is ink on fresh paper, learning old is ink on erased paper; both write
tomorrow: born without asking. so why do we still answer for it?

cards: A beginner piano class at the community center, Tuesday night. A row of keyboards. A girl whose feet don't reach the floor plays a scale without looking.
Beside her, a man with white hair and reading glasses finds middle C, loses it, finds it again. The teacher says, nice, David, and he laughs at himself.
Sooner or later somebody will ask it: isn't he a little late for this? A sage in Avot asked it first, as a riddle.

teach.b: Elisha ben Avuyah asks: one who learns as a child, what is that like? Ink written on new paper. One who learns when old, what is that like?
Ink written on erased paper. Erased paper is a page scraped and written on again. It's rougher.
The ink spreads; the old marks show. Some readers hear a warning: start young, while the page is clean. Others notice what the saying never says.
It never says the erased page refuses the ink. Both still write. A little further on, Rabbi Meir adds his own picture: don't look at the jug, look at what's in it.
A new jug can be full of old wine, and an old jug may not even hold new wine. So the jug's age tells you nothing. Open it.

Here's the part worth repeating tonight. The Talmud says Elisha himself later left the path, and calls him Acher, the other. And Rabbi Meir, his student, kept learning from him anyway, walking beside him.

teach.h: THE OLD PAGE STILL TAKES INK.
teach.b: A used page, and his student still found ink on it worth reading.
The man at the keyboard is writing on a used page. It's slower, and the notes smudge.

how: Jewish study has room for adult beginners: some synagogues and community centers teach Hebrew and text study to adults, and some adults celebrate a bar or bat mitzvah later in life.

games.q: what does “ink on new paper” mean?
o: a fresh copy of a worn-out holy book
learning young, like ink on a clean page
a rule that only children should study

games.q: the riddle of the pages — tap the pairs.
p: look inside the jug, not at it

s: Avot says only the young can really learn
it compares two pages, and both take ink. Rabbi Meir adds: look at the wine, not the jug.
the sage behind this saying is the one the Talmud later calls Acher, the other
Elisha ben Avuyah; and his student Rabbi Meir kept learning from him.

games.q: your aunt, newly retired, wants to learn Hebrew letters before a grandchild's bar mitzvah, but says her brain is old paper now. what does Avot give her?
o: the used page still takes ink, and Rabbi Meir says judge the wine, not the jug.
it's true: ink sinks in only on new paper, so she should keep her hopes low.
she should learn it fast, before the page gets any more worn than it is.
games.why: Elisha's riddle compares two pages, and both write. Rabbi Meir adds that the jug's age tells you nothing about what's inside.

practice: Pick up a pen and something to write on, and switch hands. Write today's line, both still write, slowly, with the hand you hardly use; if there's no pen nearby, trace it on your palm.
The letters wobble and the pressure is wrong, and every stroke still lands. For the rest of the sit, just look at it: a line written by a beginner.

wordCard.voice: Ink on new paper: Elisha ben Avuyah's picture of learning young. Its other half is the one to keep: erased paper takes ink too.

orig.note: Hebrew: new paper. In the riddle, the old learner's page is erased paper.

carryVoice: Something to keep from the riddle: both still write, the clean page and the used one. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:20 (Elisha ben Avuyah; numbering varies by edition)
